                                       PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                           §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                        §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                    §                OF TEXAS
                                                   §


    CRUSOE TECHNOLOGIES LLC’S COMMENTS ON STAFF’S PROPOSAL FOR
                 PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC § 25.194

         Crusoe Technologies LLC (“Crusoe”) files these comments on the Public Utility
Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Proposal for Publication (“PFP”) of the new 16 Texas
Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 25.194, relating to the rulemaking to implement large load
interconnection standards under Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) § 37.0561.

         I.        INTRODUCTION

         Crusoe is a vertically integrated artificial intelligence (“AI”) infrastructure company that
takes an “energy-first” approach to developing digital infrastructure. Crusoe has active and
planned large load projects in the ERCOT region and has participated in this rulemaking from its
inception, including filing comments on each discussion draft and participating in the January 9,
2026 workshop.
         Crusoe respectfully submits these comments on the PFP to urge the Commission to
restructure the refund provisions for financial security under the intermediate agreement and the
interconnection agreement to align refund milestones with project development milestones and
cost-causation principles.

         II.       COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSED 16 TAC § 25.194

         Crusoe appreciates the Commission’s continued engagement with stakeholders throughout
this rulemaking. Many of the changes in the PFP reflect the Commission’s thoughtful
consideration of stakeholder input. Crusoe supports a number of the revisions in the PFP, which
are discussed below. However, as identified in Section III, Crusoe has significant concerns
regarding the refund provisions for financial security and has recommended changes accordingly.




HB: 4913-0680-6682.9
        Crusoe supports the PFP’s revisions to the site control requirements at each stage of the
interconnection process. The addition of an option to purchase or lease as an acceptable form of
site control at the intermediate agreement stage reflects the commercial realities of large-scale
project development, where developers routinely secure site control through option agreements
before committing to full acquisition. Similarly, the addition of a purchase and sale agreement
(“PSA”) as an acceptable form of site control at the interconnection agreement stage appropriately
recognizes that developers may structure land transactions in a variety of ways depending on
project-specific circumstances. These changes align the rule with established industry practices
and reduce unnecessary barriers to entry for legitimate large load customers.
       Crusoe supports the reduction of required financial security (under the intermediate
agreement) and the interconnection fee (under the interconnection agreement) from $100,000/MW
to $50,000/MW. As Crusoe stated in previous comments, $50,000/MW strikes an appropriate
balance between deterring speculative load requests and avoiding excessive financial barriers that
would discourage otherwise viable projects from participating in the interconnection process.
       Crusoe also supports the PFP’s creation of distinct definitions for transmission service
provider (“TSP”) and distribution service provider (“DSP”), and the requirement that an
intermediate agreement or interconnection agreement be structured as a three-party agreement
between the large load customer, the interconnecting DSP, and the interconnecting TSP when
those entities are different. Requiring a three-party agreement in such circumstances will support
coordination between the large load customer, the interconnecting DSP, and the interconnecting
TSP. Additionally, the changes in the PFP help distinguish the roles and responsibilities of the
interconnecting TSP and interconnecting DSP.


       III.    RECOMMENDED CHANGES


               a. Refundability of Financial Commitments

       Crusoe has significant concerns about the refund provisions in the PFP.                Crusoe
recommends the Commission allow a large load customer to receive a greater refund of financial
security upon (i) withdrawal of a request, (ii) non-utilization of capacity, or (iii) energization and
achievement of project milestones. While Crusoe supports the policy goal of screening out


                                            Page 2 of 34
                                          HB: 4913-0680-6682.9
 speculative load requests, the PFP’s provision allowing a customer to receive only a 20% refund
of financial security upon withdrawal of an interconnection request is not necessary to deter
speculative load requests, as the requirement to post financial security at $50,000 per MW of
requested peak demand is itself a sufficient deterrent.
       The magnitude of the financial commitment required under the PFP effectively eliminates
speculative actors from the process. For example, a large load customer seeking 500 MW of
capacity must post $25 million in financial security before any study is conducted. The customer
must make this commitment upon execution of the intermediate agreement, before receiving any
information about available transmission capacity, required system upgrades, or achievable
energization timelines, and before the customer has any assurance that its project is viable at the
proposed site. A speculative actor is unlikely to post $25 million under these conditions. The
financial security requirement alone accomplishes the Legislature’s objective of discouraging
speculative requests.
       The PFP’s 80/20 refund structure goes far beyond deterrence. Under the current provisions,
the TSP may retain 80% of a customer’s financial security upon withdrawal of an interconnection
request, without any requirement that the retained amount must have a nexus to costs actually
incurred. This imposes a disproportionate financial burden on large load customers, which is not
supported by cost-causation principles.


                        i. Refundability of Intermediate Agreement Financial Commitments

       Crusoe recommends that the Commission allow a large load customer that voluntarily
withdraws its interconnection request before executing an interconnection agreement to receive a
full refund of all financial security, minus only the actual, documented costs incurred by the
interconnecting DSP or TSP in processing the request. A customer that withdraws at this stage has
not caused the interconnecting DSP or TSP to incur costs beyond those associated with processing
and studying the request. Retaining any portion of the financial security in excess of those actual
costs is punitive and lacks a policy justification.
       In addition to providing a full refund upon voluntary withdrawal, the Commission should
also provide for a refund of financial security attributable to requested peak demand that cannot
be served. If an interconnection study determines that the grid cannot reliably serve the customer’s


                                             Page 3 of 34
                                           HB: 4913-0680-6682.9
 full requested peak demand, the customer should receive a refund of financial security attributable
to the MWs that cannot be served. For example, if a customer requests 500 MW but the
interconnection study determines that only 250 MW can be allocated, and the customer elects to
proceed with that partial allocation, the customer must execute an interconnection agreement for
250 MW and pay an interconnection fee of $12.5 million. Under the proposed 16 TAC
§25.194(f)(7)(A), the interconnecting DSP or TSP must draw on the $25 million already posted
under the intermediate agreement to satisfy this fee, leaving a balance of $12.5 million—all of
which is attributable to the 250 MW that ERCOT determined cannot be served. The customer
should receive a full refund of that remaining $12.5 million, as it no longer serves any purpose in
the interconnection process.
       The PFP does not provide a mechanism for refunding financial security attributable to
MWs that cannot be served. Refund of intermediate agreement financial security is governed by
subsection (g), which permits only a 20% refund upon voluntary withdrawal and allows the TSP
to retain the remaining 80%. The customer cannot obtain a refund for non-utilization of capacity
under subsection (h) or for achieving energization under subsection (i), even though other forms
of financial security are refundable under those subsections. Moreover, subsection (g) addresses
only voluntary withdrawal; it does not contemplate a scenario in which the interconnection study
determines that a portion of requested peak demand cannot be served.
       There is no regulatory justification for withholding financial security under these
circumstances. The customer has not abandoned its request, the unallocated MWs will not be
served, and the remaining financial security will mitigate the cost risk associated with the MWs
that will actually be interconnected. Crusoe recommends that the Commission revise the proposed
16 TAC §25.194 to expressly provide that any portion of intermediate agreement financial security
attributable to requested peak demand that cannot be served, as determined in the interconnection
study, shall be refunded to the large load customer within 60 days of execution of the
interconnection agreement.




                                           Page 4 of 34
                                         HB: 4913-0680-6682.9
                        ii. Refundability       of     Interconnection     Agreement       Financial
                           Commitments

       The Commission should also revise the refund provisions applicable to financial security
posted under the interconnection agreement. The PFP’s 80/20 refund structure for financial
security allows a TSP to retain a disproportionate percentage of financial security posted by a large
load customer that has energized and otherwise performed under its interconnection agreement.
The proposed §25.194(i)(1) provides that upon energization, the interconnecting DSP or TSP must
refund only 20% of the remaining balance of financial security, and thereafter must do so ratably
as the customer meets the milestones identified in its interconnection agreement. Under
§25.194(i)(2), the TSP or DSP must then refund “any remaining balance” once the customer has
sustained operations for five years at its contracted peak demand. The practical effect is that the
TSP may retain the customer’s financial security for years, even when the customer has met every
obligation under its interconnection agreement and the large load is energized.
       If the purpose of the $50,000/MW security is to ensure that large load customers pay their
fair share of transmission system upgrades, then that objective is properly accomplished through
the transmission cost of service (“TCOS”) allocation methodology, not by requiring certain retail
customers to pre-fund transmission upgrades through financial security. The Commission is
already addressing the TCOS allocation methodology in Project No. 58484. Allowing customer
financial security to offset a TSP’s rate base effectively imposes a surcharge on large load
customers that does not have a nexus to the actual costs that those customers cause. As discussed
below, Crusoe recommends that the Commission revise the proposed rule to provide that 50% of
a customer’s remaining financial security shall be refunded when the customer energizes, and
thereafter the security will continue to be refunded as the customer meets the load ramp milestones
established in its interconnection agreement, so that a customer receives a full refund once it
reaches contracted peak demand.
       Crusoe also urges the Commission to make the interconnection fee refundable, in line with
financial security paid under the intermediate and interconnection agreements. It is particularly
problematic that, under the PFP, the refundable $50,000/MW financial security paid under the
intermediate agreement is later transferred into a nonrefundable $50,000/MW interconnection fee
under the interconnection agreement. As the customer energizes, achieves load ramp milestones,


                                           Page 5 of 34
                                          HB: 4913-0680-6682.9
 and eventually reaches its full contracted peak demand, there is no remaining justification for the
TSP to retain the $50,000/MW interconnection fee as a nonrefundable payment, since direct
interconnection costs are covered through CIAC and system upgrades are covered through the
financial security that must be posted for such upgrades.


                       iii. Refund Related to Achieving Energization

       The Commission should ensure that a large load customer that has energized its load
receives a meaningful refund of financial security, rather than being subject to the PFP’s punitive
forfeiture structure. The nonrefundable financial security structure is premised on the assumption
that large load customers may abandon their projects after energization, but this assumption is
contradicted by the economic realities of large-scale infrastructure development. A developer that
has reached energization has, by definition, committed substantial capital to site acquisition,
equipment procurement, construction, and interconnection. These expenditures may dwarf the
financial security itself. The real deterrent to project abandonment is the developer’s own sunk
cost, not the threat of forfeiting a fraction of its total investment. By way of public example,
Crusoe’s financing for its Abilene, Texas data center was approximately $3.4 billion. A developer
that has invested billions of dollars in a facility and successfully energized its load is hardly likely
to abandon that facility. The nonrefundable fee structure thus imposes a penalty on the very
developers who have demonstrated the strongest commitment to the ERCOT system, while
providing no deterrent effect beyond what the developer’s own capital investment already
provides.
       Crusoe recommends that the Commission replace the 80/20 forfeiture structure with a
phased refund framework for financial security and the interconnection fee that aligns refund
milestones with the customer’s demonstrated commitment to the project. Specifically: (1) upon
initial energization of the first phase of the project, 50% of remaining financial security (minus
actual costs incurred) shall be refunded; (2) the remaining financial security (minus actual costs
incurred) shall be refunded ratably as the customer successfully meets the energization milestones
established in the interconnection agreement; and (3) a full refund of all remaining security (minus
actual costs) shall be made upon the customer reaching its contracted peak demand level. This
structure preserves the deterrent effect of the financial security requirement during the period when


                                             Page 6 of 34
                                           HB: 4913-0680-6682.9
 speculative risk is highest (that is, before energization), while ensuring that developer capital is
not permanently diverted to offset a TSP’s rate base once the developer has demonstrated that its
project is real and operational.
       Additionally, the interconnection fee should apply only to new large load interconnection
requests, not to incremental capacity additions by existing customers. A project that has been
operational for an extended period and subsequently requests additional load does not pose a
speculative load risk. Imposing the full $50,000/MW financial security requirement (under the
intermediate agreement) and $50,000/MW interconnection fee (under the interconnection
agreement) on such incremental requests would penalize customers for growing their operations
in the ERCOT region, an outcome that is contrary to the Legislature’s intent in enacting PURA §
37.0561.


       IV.     CONCLUSION

       The PFP’s financial security provisions, as currently drafted, impose costs on large load
customers that are disproportionate to the risks that they are designed to mitigate. The provisions
also create ambiguities that may result in unjust forfeiture of customer capital and permit customer
security to flow to a TSP’s rate base in a manner inconsistent with cost-causation principles.
Crusoe urges the Commission to adopt the revisions set forth above to ensure that the final rule
accomplishes the Legislature’s objective of deterring speculative interconnection requests without
imposing punitive financial consequences on developers that demonstrate genuine commitment to
building load in the ERCOT region. A financial security framework that refunds developer capital
as milestones are met will promote, rather than discourage, the large-scale investment in Texas
that PURA § 37.0561 was enacted to facilitate.
       Crusoe appreciates the Commission’s consideration of these important issues and urges
adoption of a final rule that supports innovation, investment, and reliability in Texas.

      §25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.
(a)   Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility,

      a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative to interconnect a large load customer

      to the ERCOT system. Nothing in this section limits the authority of a municipally owned

      utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load

      customers on their systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section.



(b)   Applicability. This section applies to a large load customer that seeks:

      (1)    a new interconnection that is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts (MW);

      (2)    an expanded interconnection that equals or exceeds 75 MW for the first time; and

      (3)    an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.



(c)   Definitions. The following words and terms, when used in this section, have the following

      meanings unless the context indicates otherwise:

      (1)    Backup generating facilities -- Generation facilities or energy storage facilities

             that are not capable of operating, or are not configured to operate, in parallel with

             the ERCOT system and cannot export energy to the ERCOT system.

      (2)    Competitively sensitive information -- Competitively sensitive information

             includes exact site locations, such as parcel identifiers or property boundaries;

             commercial terms, such as pricing or internal development prioritization;

             proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-deployment strategies; and


                                          Page 9 of 34
                                        HB: 4913-0680-6682.9
       financing structures. Competitively sensitive information does not include the

      identity of a large load customer; general site location, such as load zone; requested

      or contracted peak demand; timing of energization; or whether an interconnection

      request is associated with the same applicant or affiliated entities.

(3)   Contracted peak demand -- The total non-coincident peak demand that a large

      load customer requests that an interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP

      serve at a site as stated interconnection agreement.

(4)   Interconnecting distribution service provider (DSP) -- The electric utility,

      municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that is certificated to provide

      retail electric delivery service at the location in which the large load customer seeks

      to interconnect.

(5)   Interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP) -- The electric utility,

      municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that owns and operates the

      facilities necessary to interconnect the large load customer to the ERCOT system.

(6)   Interconnection agreement -- An agreement that is executed by a large load

      customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different from the interconnecting DSP,

      the interconnecting TSP after completion of the interconnection study and that, at

      a minimum, satisfies subsection (f) of this section.

(7)   Interconnection study -- The set of studies that are required by ERCOT before a

      large load customer may be interconnected.

(8)   Intermediate agreement -- An agreement that is executed by a large load

      customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different from the interconnecting DSP,




                                  Page 10 of 34

              the interconnecting TSP before the interconnection study are initiated and that, at a

             minimum, satisfies subsection (d) of this section.

      (9)    Large load customer -- An entity requesting a new or expanded interconnection

             where the customer’s total expected non-coincident peak demand at a single site is

             equal to or exceeds 75 MW.

      (10)   Requested peak demand -- The total non-coincident peak demand that a large load

             customer requests, prior to executing an interconnection agreement, that an

             interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP serve at a site.



(d)   Intermediate agreement. Before a new large load interconnection request is submitted to

      ERCOT for study, the large load customer must execute an intermediate agreement with

      the interconnecting DSP and, if different from the interconnecting DSP, the interconnecting

      TSP. If the interconnecting DSP and the interconnecting TSP are different entities, the

      intermediate agreement must specifically identify each entity’s responsibilities under this

      section, including which entity will accept the study fee and financial security from the

      large load customer. The intermediate agreement must meet the requirements of this

      subsection.

      (1)    Site control. A large load customer must demonstrate site control for the proposed

             load location through provision of one of the following property interests to the

             interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP:

             (A)     a signed and executed lease agreement for one or more parcels of land

                     sufficient to accommodate the customer’s planned facilities at the proposed

              load location for a duration of at least five years from the date the large load

             customer is expected to reach the contracted peak demand;

      (B)    a deed for one or more parcels of land sufficient to accommodate the

             customer’s planned facilities at the proposed load location; or

      (C)    a signed and executed agreement with an option to purchase or lease one or

             more parcels of land sufficient to accommodate the customer’s planned

             facilities at the proposed location.

(2)   Substantially similar interconnection request. A large load customer must

      disclose to the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP whether the

      customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request for electric

      service, the approval of which would result in the customer materially changing,

      delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection request. A material change or delay

      includes a delay of one or more years to the project’s projected date to realize its

      requested or contracted peak demand, a 20% or greater change in the requested or

      contracted peak demand, or a change in the location for the point of interconnection.

      (A)    A large load customer that is pursuing a substantially similar

             interconnection request for electric service the approval of which would

             result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the

             interconnection request must disclose the following information to the

             interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP:

             (i)     the ERCOT-assigned serial number (i.e., the large load

                     interconnection      number)      for   the    substantially    similar

                     interconnection request, as applicable;

       (ii)    the location, including the power region and, if in the ERCOT

              region, the load zone, of the substantially similar interconnection

              request;

      (iii)   the non-coincident peak demand of the substantially similar

              interconnection request;

      (iv)    the anticipated timing of energization of the substantially similar

              interconnection request; and

      (v)     the interconnecting DSP and, if different from the interconnecting

(B)   A large load customer that discloses a substantially similar interconnection

        Crusoe supports the PFP's revisions to the site control requirements at each stage of the

security upon (i) withdrawal of a request, (ii) non-utilization of capacity, or (iii) energization and

which is attributable to the 250 MW that ERCOT determined cannot be served. The customer
should receive a full refund of that remaining $12.5 million, as it no longer serves any purpose in
the interconnection process.

MWs that cannot be served. Refund of intermediate agreement financial security is governed by
subsection (g), which permits only a 20% refund upon voluntary withdrawal and allows the TSP
to retain the remaining 80%. The customer cannot obtain a refund for non-utilization of capacity
under subsection (h) or for achieving energization under subsection (i), even though other forms
of financial security are refundable under those subsections. Moreover, subsection (g) addresses
only voluntary withdrawal; it does not contemplate a scenario in which the interconnection study
determines that a portion of requested peak demand cannot be served.
       There is no regulatory justification for withholding financial security under these
circumstances. The customer has not abandoned its request, the unallocated MWs will not be
served, and the remaining financial security will mitigate the cost risk associated with the MWs
that will actually be interconnected. Crusoe recommends that the Commission revise the proposed
16 TAC §25.194 to expressly provide that any portion ofintermediate agreement financial security
attributable to requested peak demand that cannot be served, as determined in the interconnection

       The Commission should also revise the refund provisions applicable to financial security
posted under the interconnection agreement. The PFP' s 80/20 refund structure for financial
security allows a TSP to retain a disproportionate percentage of financial security posted by a large
load customer that has energized and otherwise performed under its interconnection agreement.
The proposed §25.194(i)(1) provides that upon energization, the interconnecting DSP or TSP must
refund only 20% of the remaining balance of financial security, and thereafter must do so ratably
as the customer meets the milestones identified in its interconnection agreement. Under
§25.194(i)(2), the TSP or DSP must then refund "any remaining balance" once the customer has
sustained operations for five years at its contracted peak demand. The practical effect is that the
TSP may retain the customer' s financial security for years, even when the customer has met every
obligation under its interconnection agreement and the large load is energized.
       If the purpose of the $50,000/MW security is to ensure that large load customers pay their
fair share of transmission system upgrades, then that objective is properly accomplished through
the transmission cost of service ("TCOS") allocation methodology, not by requiring certain retail
customers to pre-fund transmission upgrades through financial security. The Commission is
already addressing the TCOS allocation methodology in Project No. 58484. Allowing customer
financial security to offset a TSP's rate base effectively imposes a surcharge on large load
customers that does not have a nexus to the actual costs that those customers cause. As discussed
below, Crusoe recommends that the Commission revise the proposed rule to provide that 50% of
a customer' s remaining financial security shall be refunded when the customer energizes, and
thereafter the security will continue to be refunded as the customer meets the load ramp milestones
established in its interconnection agreement, so that a customer receives a full refund once it
reaches contracted peak demand.
       Crusoe also urges the Commission to make the interconnection fee refundable, in line with
financial security paid under the intermediate and interconnection agreements. It is particularly
problematic that, under the PFP, the refundable $50,000/MW financial security paid under the
intermediate agreement is later transferred into a nonrefundable $50,000/MW interconnection fee
under the interconnection agreement. As the customer energizes, achieves load ramp milestones,

TSP to retain the $50,000/MW interconnection fee as a nonrefundable payment, since direct
interconnection costs are covered through CIAC and system upgrades are covered through the
financial security that must be posted for such upgrades.


                       iii. Refund Related to Achieving Energization


        The Commission should ensure that a large load customer that has energized its load
receives a meaningful refund of financial security, rather than being subject to the PFP's punitive
forfeiture structure. The nonrefundable financial security structure is premised on the assumption
that large load customers may abandon their projects after energization, but this assumption is
contradicted by the economic realities of large-scale infrastructure development. A developer that
has reached energization has, by definition, committed substantial capital to site acquisition,
equipment procurement, construction, and interconnection. These expenditures may dwarf the
financial security itself. The real deterrent to project abandonment is the developer' s own sunk
cost, not the threat of forfeiting a fraction of its total investment. By way of public example,
Crusoe's financing for its Abilene, Texas data center was approximately $3.4 billion. A developer
that has invested billions of dollars in a facility and successfully energized its load is hardly likely
to abandon that facility. The nonrefundable fee structure thus imposes a penalty on the very
developers who have demonstrated the strongest commitment to the ERCOT system, while
providing no deterrent effect beyond what the developer' s own capital investment already
provides.
        Crusoe recommends that the Commission replace the 80/20 forfeiture structure with a
phased refund framework for financial security and the interconnection fee that aligns refund
milestones with the customer' s demonstrated commitment to the project. Specifically: (1) upon
initial energization of the first phase of the project, 50% of remaining financial security (minus
actual costs incurred) shall be refunded; (2) the remaining financial security (minus actual costs
incurred) shall be refunded ratably as the customer successfully meets the energization milestones
established in the interconnection agreement; and (3) a full refund of all remaining security (minus
actual costs) shall be made upon the customer reaching its contracted peak demand level. This
structure preserves the deterrent effect ofthe financial security requirement during the period when

 speculative risk is highest (that is, before energization), while ensuring that developer capital is
not permanently diverted to offset a TSP' s rate base once the developer has demonstrated that its
project is real and operational.
       Additionally, the interconnection fee should apply only to new large load interconnection
requests, not to incremental capacity additions by existing customers. A proj ect that has been
operational for an extended period and subsequently requests additional load does not pose a
speculative load risk. Imposing the full $50,000/MW financial security requirement (under the
intermediate agreement) and $50,000/MW interconnection fee (under the interconnection
agreement) on such incremental requests would penalize customers for growing their operations
in the ERCOT region, an outcome that is contrary to the Legislature's intent in enacting PURA §
37.0561.


       IV.      CONCLUSION

        The PFP's financial security provisions, as currently drafted, impose costs on large load
customers that are disproportionate to the risks that they are designed to mitigate. The provisions
also create ambiguities that may result in unjust forfeiture of customer capital and permit customer
security to flow to a TSP' s rate base in a manner inconsistent with cost-causation principles.
Crusoe urges the Commission to adopt the revisions set forth above to ensure that the final rule
accomplishes the Legislature' s objective of deterring speculative interconnection requests without
imposing punitive financial consequences on developers that demonstrate genuine commitment to
building load in the ERCOT region. A financial security framework that refunds developer capital
as milestones are met will promote, rather than discourage, the large-scale investment in Texas
that PURA § 37.0561 was enacted to facilitate.
        Crusoe appreciates the Commission's consideration of these important issues and urges
adoption of a final rule that supports innovation, investment, and reliability in Texas.

                             EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Crusoe supports the PFP' s revisions to site control requirements, the reduction of financial
security to $50,000/MW, and the distinction between the interconnecting DSP and TSP,
including the requirement for a three-party interconnection or intermediate agreement
where those entities differ.

Crusoe urges the Commission to revise the PFP's 80/20 forfeiture structure, which goes
far beyond deterrence. The $50,000/MW financial security requirement alone is sufficient
to deter speculative interconnection requests. The 80/20 structure allows the TSP to retain
financial security without any nexus to costs actually incurred, imposing a disproportionate
burden not supported by cost-causation principles.

Crusoe recommends that the Commission allow a customer to receive a full refund of
intermediate agreement financial security attributable to any MWs that cannot be served,
as identified in the interconnection study. This refund should be made within 60 days of
execution ofthe interconnection agreement.

Crusoe recommends that a large load customer that voluntarily withdraws before executing
an interconnection agreement should receive a full refund of all financial security, minus
only actual, documented costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or TSP.

Crusoe urges the Commission to revise the interconnection agreement refund provisions to
replace the 80/20 forfeiture structure with a phased refund framework: (1) 50% upon initial
energization; (2) ratably as the customer meets energization milestones; and (3) in full once
the customer achieves contracted peak demand. The interconnection fee should also be
made refundable on the same basis.

The $50,000/MW financial security requirement and the interconnection fee should not
apply to incremental capacity additions by existing customers.
